beats.text: Look at the back wall of this room, just above the round mirror. There, in ornate Latin script, a line of writing runs across the wall. In English it says, Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.
So the painter tells us, in his own lettering, that he stood in this room in that year. But another date sits uneasily beside it.
The woman most often named as the wife in green is Costanza Trenta, first wife of the merchant Giovanni Arnolfini. She died in 1433, a full year before the date on the wall.
This small panel is crowded with detail, and repeated close looking has not settled what it means. So which is it, a wedding happening in front of us, or a memory of a woman already gone?
Let your eye drop from the lettering, past the mirror, to the two people standing in the room below.

Start with the man on the left, under the dark hat. An early inventory names him Hernoul le Fin. Most historians take him to be Giovanni Arnolfini, an Italian merchant in Bruges, the right age in 1434.
His family came from Lucca in Tuscany to Bruges, a hub of trade in fifteenth-century Flanders. They seem to have mixed trade with finance, among the first merchant bankers.
Now look at the woman in green. What is known of Costanza Trenta is brief. She married Giovanni in 1426, they had no recorded children, and she died in 1433.

So is this Costanza, as some historians think? Others see a second wife, married after Costanza died, though no record of her has been found. It has also been suggested the panel was begun in Costanza's lifetime and finished after her death.
Either way, why would a merchant want a picture like this? Booming trade had raised a new merchant class hungry for status. In the 1430s, a portrait by Van Eyck was the most exclusive way to show it.

It is also among the earliest portraits of a couple neither royal nor noble, shown at home rather than at court. It seems built to fix their place in the new middle class. And the first thing they show us is what they wear.

Begin with the woman's green dress. She gathers its full, high-waisted front in her hand, though she is not shown as pregnant. Dyeing wool this even green is thought to have kept a team of dyers busy for weeks.
The gown is lined with squirrel fur, which shows pale at the cuffs. One estimate puts it at 2,000 pieces of belly fur, where 600 was usual.
Near the hem, a little blue appears, an underdress trimmed with white fur. Blue was costly and tied to the Virgin Mary, and she shows only a little.
Her frilled white headdress marks her as married, since unmarried women wore their hair loose. Her jewelry is kept modest.
Now cross to Giovanni, in dark plum. Dark dyes cost more than light ones. Whether the plum lies in his fabrics or his fur is debated, and the colours have faded.

His tabard, a sleeveless outer garment, is likely silk velvet from Lucca, lined with pine marten. The lining may have taken a hundred Russian martens, close in cost to sable, a fur kept for aristocrats.
His straw hat, woven in tiny plaits, is a new Italian fashion. His soft boots show the shape of his feet.
Giovanni grew rich, it seems, trading silks and luxury fabrics. So the couple wear the kind of goods Flanders traded, a walking advert for his business.
One reading sees this wealth shown with care, never quite aristocratic. Another sees it laid out openly, every choice made to broadcast it. The room around them makes the same claim.
Start with the bed behind the couple, hung in deep red. It suggests a bedroom, but this was most likely a reception room.
One reading sees a costly bed for show, never slept in. Another notes that in Burgundy, beds were used as seating.
Behind the joined hands stands a bench called a settle, its red velvet cushion a sign of money. Carved gargoyles, thought to ward off evil spirits, sit above those hands.

On the high-backed chair beside it, a carved woman stands on a dragon. Some historians see Saint Martha, patron of housewives, her brush hanging nearby. Others see Saint Margaret, patron of childbirth.
On the floor lies an Anatolian rug, rare and costly in northern Europe. Such carpets often appear in paintings of the Virgin, so it may also hint at piety.
Beside the mirror hang amber prayer beads, a common gift from groom to bride. Each bead catches the light, strung on fine green silk.
The window glass at left, itself a luxury, has been called crown glass and stained glass. Beyond it, a cherry tree in fruit suggests early summer.

Oranges lie on the sill and chest, imported fruit only the wealthy could afford. The single orange on the sill casts a shadow and shows in the glass behind it. It is a still life, painted before still life was a genre.
Above them hangs a gleaming brass chandelier. Yet every line here seems to lead the eye to one object, the mirror.
Come closer to the round mirror on the back wall. Its glass bulges outward, as costly glass mirrors did then.
A mirror this large could not yet be made, so the painter seems to have scaled it up.

In the reflection we see the couple from behind, and two small figures in the doorway. They stand where we stand, outside the picture, and Giovanni raises his right hand toward them, seemingly in greeting.
So who are they? The figure in blue is often taken to be the painter himself. The other has been read as his assistant, or as a stand-in for us.
If that is Van Eyck, he was court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, in Bruges. His service is dated to 1425 or 1426. The duke paid him a yearly salary and sent him on diplomatic missions.
Now look at the frame. Ten tiny roundels circle the glass, each a scene from the Passion of Christ. Among them are the Agony in the Garden, the Flagellation and the Crucifixion.
Together they have been read as God's promise of salvation. The spotless glass itself is read as purity. Some tie it to the Virgin Mary, others to the sanctity of the marriage.
But notice where the scenes fall. Those after Christ's death, the Descent from the Cross, the Entombment, the Resurrection and the Harrowing of Hell, all sit on the woman's side.
Why would death and rising gather beside her, and not beside him?
In 1934 the art historian Erwin Panofsky proposed that this panel served as a legal record of a marriage. Look at the joined hands at the centre. To him the pose recalled the taking of vows.
Then lift your eye to the inscription. Its words, Jan van Eyck was here, sound like a witness signing an official record. Yet they have also been read as one of his witty signatures.
Now drop to the lower left, where his pointed overshoes, called pattens, lie on the floor. A second pair stands farther back.
One reading links them to a line in the Book of Exodus, where shoes come off on holy ground. Others see the sanctity of marriage, or his life outside and hers at home.
Then come signs read as love and fertility, the oranges, the cherry tree, the green of her dress. The gathered skirt has been read as a fertility pose, and as plain fashion of the day.
Even the chandelier joins in. Only one candle is lit, and it has been read as the seeing eye of God.
The memorial reading starts from the same hands. One historian sees Giovanni holding hers tentatively, as if she were slipping from his grasp.
At her feet sits a dog. It can mean loyalty. But it also recalls dogs carved at women's feet on tombs, meant to go with them into the afterlife.
His dark clothes may be mourning dress. And the scenes after Christ's death gather on her side of the mirror.
Some even read the fertility signs as a hint that she died in childbirth.
Both cases rest on the same pair of hands, read two ways. The marriage reading is now disputed, the memorial one more recent, and neither closes the question.
Now set meaning aside, and simply look at the surface. Light from the window at left falls both direct and soft. It glints on the brass chandelier, the mirror and the white frills of her headdress.
How did he make it shine like this? Van Eyck mixed pigment with linseed oil, and laid it on in many thin, see-through layers called glazes.
Picture sheets of tinted glass stacked together, light passing through each. The glazes work roughly like that, leaving the panel smooth and luminous.
He also worked fresh paint into paint still wet, and used a nearly dry brush for fine textures.
He did not invent oil painting, but he was among the first to use it, and he refined it. His contemporaries called him an alchemist.
Yet only some twenty-three paintings are thought to be by his hand alone.
He built in symbols for us to hunt, yet some objects, like these amber beads, are simply painted superbly.
Look back at the woman in green, in that same light. Is she alive in it, or only remembered?
Lift your eye once more to the line above the mirror, Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.
So is this a wedding or a memory? The hands, the shoes and the fruit can speak of a marriage. The dog, the dark clothes and the scenes on her side can speak of a loss.
The hinge is the woman, and she cannot be named for certain. If she is Costanza, this is a memory. If she is a second wife, no record of her has been found.
His work was sought after in England, France and Portugal. Painters from Dürer to the Pre-Raphaelites seem to have learned from him, Velázquez among them in Las Meninas of 1656.
In the mirror, two figures still stand in the doorway, where we stand.
